lesson.grammar_point: future forms for prediction: will (opinion), be going to (evidence), be likely to / be expected to (probability), future continuous (will be doing: in progress at a future time)

listenings.text: Every January, my clients ask me the same question. What's going to happen this year? And every January, I give the same honest answer. I don't know exactly, but I can tell you what's likely. Here's my view for heavy industry in the Americas. Demand for trucks and machinery is likely to grow, but slowly. Interest rates are expected to come down a little, which usually helps investment. Infrastructure is the big opportunity. Ports, railways and energy will need a lot of steel and a lot of castings. The biggest risk is uncertainty. When companies don't know what will happen, they wait. So my advice is simple. Don't plan for the best case. Plan for steady growth, and be ready to move fast if the market recovers sooner than expected.

I'm the finance director of a car parts company in Mumbai, and half of our sales are in dollars. So the exchange rate is something I think about every single day. People often ask me for a forecast. Will our currency be stronger or weaker next year? My answer is that nobody knows, and anyone who says they know is selling something. What we do instead is prepare three scenarios. In the good one, the currency stays stable and our margins improve. In the bad one, it falls quickly and our costs go up. And in the middle one, which is the most likely, it moves a little every month. This time next year, we'll still be talking about the exchange rate. That's the only forecast I'm sure about.

I've worked in mining for twenty-five years, and I've learned to look at trends, not at headlines. Headlines change every week. Trends take ten years. And the trend right now is clear. The world is going to need more metal, not less. Electric cars, wind farms and new power lines all use huge amounts of copper, aluminum and steel. Will there be bad years? Of course. There will be slowdowns, and prices will go up and down. But over the next decade, demand is likely to grow. So when a client from Brazil or from Japan asks me if it's a good moment to invest, I always ask them back. Are you thinking about next quarter, or about the next ten years?
